rashi:a1.1: Mishna. Animal tithe etc. With sheep and with goats: that is, and it is in effect with sheep and goats.
rashi:a2.1: New: those born after [the first of] Elul.
rashi:a2.3: And new and old are not tithed from one for the other: as the Gemara explains.
rashi:a3.1: Gemara. Let us say the mishna: which teaches that it is in effect outside the Land.
rashi:a4.1: Tithe of grain: is in effect only in the Land, as we say in the first chapter of Kiddushin (37a): every mitzva that is an obligation of the land is in effect only in the Land; and we derive it from verses.
rashi:a5.1: To be sacrificed: [Rabbi Akiva excludes it from being sacrificed,] not from becoming sacred. And the mishna, which teaches that it is in effect, means that it becomes sacred; and the Gemara explains shortly for what halakha it is sacred.
rashi:a5.2: The language is also precise: that Rabbi Akiva excludes it from sacrifice, since the teaching takes his statement from “and you shall bring there,” which is sacrifice.
rashi:a6.1: With its blemish: he waits until it becomes blemished and eats it. Animal tithe, whether unblemished or blemished, belongs to the owners, since we find no verse saying it is given to the priest.
rashi:a7.1: In accordance with Rav Huna, who said: later in this chapter (Bekhorot 58b).
rashi:a7.2: A decree due to an orphan: here too [nowadays] it is a decree due to an orphan, lest one bring an orphan into the pen to be tithed; for the mishna [58b] says: all enter the pen to be tithed except diverse kinds, a tereifa, one born by caesarean section, one lacking in time [too young] and an orphan. Rav Huna names the orphan rather than any of the others because there, in the context of his statement, only “a purchased animal and an orphan” are relevant, later in this chapter. An orphan: whose mother died at the time of birth, “this one departed to death and that one departed to life.”
rashi:a8.1: Originally too: when the Temple stood, let us decree due to an orphan.
rashi:a8.2: Rather: the reason we did not decree in the time of the Temple is that it was possible by an announcement of the court that no one bring an orphan into the pen to be tithed. So nowadays too, let them separate it, since an announcement is possible.
rashi:a9.1: Due to a mishap: since we have nowhere to sacrifice, he would have to keep it until it becomes blemished, and he would come to a mishap with it: shearing it and working it, or slaughtering it without a blemish.
rashi:a9.2: Nor dedicate [maḥarimin]: for a dedication [ḥerem] is sacred like consecrated property, as it is written: “every devoted thing is most holy” (Leviticus 27:28).
rashi:a10.1: It should be uprooted: so that one not come to a mishap with it.
rashi:a10.2: It dies on its own: of hunger.
rashi:a11.1: Does the firstborn depend on us? Said in astonishment.
rashi:a11.2: This is what he is saying: this is our challenge: since you are concerned about a mishap, let us transfer ownership of the mothers’ ears to gentiles, so that a gentile has a hand in it, and it will not come to firstborn status.
rashi:b1.1: And it answers: it is possible by another remedy, as Rabbi Yehuda says. And this remedy is better than that one, as we said in the first chapter (above, Bekhorot 3b): that is why Rav Mari’s animals died out, because he used to transfer ownership of their ears to a gentile, since that removes them even from the priest’s holiness [i.e., the priest loses his gift].
rashi:b1.2: Here too: with tithe, a remedy is possible that does not require keeping it: let him inflict a blemish on it from the outset.
rashi:b2.1: And it answers: who knows which will come out?
rashi:b2.2: At the head of ten: as the tenth.
rashi:b2.3: He shall not inquire: implies that he must not bring it out [himself]; rather, it comes out on its own.
rashi:b3.1: And if you say it is possible to inflict a blemish on his entire herd: before he tithes, while they are still non-sacred and it is permitted to inflict a blemish; and afterward he tithes, for the tithe takes effect on a blemished animal, as it is written: “He shall not inquire whether it be good or bad” (Leviticus 27:33).
rashi:b4.1: And it challenges: here too, with a firstborn, where you said he may inflict a blemish on them, one can challenge: soon the Temple will be rebuilt, etc.
rashi:b5.1: Here too it is possible with purchased animals: for purchased animals need no blemish inflicted on them, since they are exempt from the tithe, as the mishna [55b] teaches: an animal purchased or received as a gift is exempt from animal tithe.
rashi:b5.2: And it answers: since he inflicts blemishes on his whole herd, the exempt ones among his animals, the purchased ones, are few. And blemishes that disqualify for offerings are very common; even the dukin of the eye [Davidson: the eyelid] disqualify. So animals fit to be sacrificed would not be common, and for this reason we do not separate the tithe.
rashi:b7.1: And in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: it was needed to teach us to include offerings of lesser sanctity: if one deposited peace-offering animals with his fellow, and the fellow denied it and swore, and afterward admitted, he pays the principal and a fifth and brings a guilt offering. For we read of it “against the Lord” and “against his fellow,” as it is written: “And he commits a trespass against the Lord and denies to his fellow” (Leviticus 5:21), and peace offerings have a share for the Lord and a share for one’s fellow.
rashi:b8.1: Here too: let them be tithed.
rashi:b8.2: Shall be sacred: the tenth shall be sacred.
rashi:b9.1: The sanctity of the tithe: the Gemara explains below: and he would transgress with them “it shall not be sold” and “it shall not be redeemed.”
rashi:b10.1: From sanctity to sanctity: the sanctity of the altar does not take effect on sanctity for Temple maintenance, even though the altar’s sanctity is more stringent; nor does the sanctity of Temple maintenance take effect on the altar’s sanctity such that he would have to give their value to Temple maintenance.
rashi:b10.2: But one may consecrate: altar offerings for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b10.3: Consecration of value: the benefit [tovat hana’a] he has from the altar’s sanctity he can give to Temple maintenance. That benefit is that he could take a sela from another Israelite on condition that he give the animal to that man’s daughter’s son, a priest, to sacrifice it, as we said in chapter Ad Kamma (above, Bekhorot 27a). Ileui [value] means that he assesses that measure of benefit in money and gives it to the Temple treasurer.
rashi:b10.4: And they dedicate them: they dedicate altar offerings, and he gives the priest according to the benefit he has in them; but on the altar’s own portion no other sanctity takes effect.
rashi:b11.1: Lest you say: the reason the altar’s sanctity does not take effect on the sanctity of Temple maintenance is that not every animal stands to be a burnt offering, since most animals stand to be eaten. Therefore when he consecrated it for Temple maintenance, he consecrated it properly, and the sanctity of Temple maintenance took full effect on it, so that it can no longer be changed to an altar offering. But with tithe, where every animal stands to be tithe, even though he consecrated it as a peace offering, the law of tithe is not removed from it.
rashi:b12.1: And what difference does it make, if the sanctity of tithe took effect on a peace offering? For tithe is not more stringent than a peace offering.
rashi:b12.2: To make it subject to “it shall not be sold” and “it shall not be redeemed”: for peace offerings can be redeemed [when blemished]. It teaches us: “shall be sacred,” and not what is already sacred.
rashi:b14.1: Just as grain tithe is not taken from the new for the old: as it is written (Deuteronomy 14:22): “that the field brings forth year by year.” From what comes out in a year you tithe, and not from this year for the past year, nor from the past year for the coming year.
rashi:b15.1: Just as grain tithe is not taken from one type for another: as we say below: give the best of this and the best of that.
rashi:b15.2: And flock: implies that all flock counts as one species with regard to tithe.
rashi:b16.1: But it is written: You shall tithe a tithe: which is juxtaposed to the grain tithe.
rashi:b16.2: I juxtaposed it with regard to the year: animal tithe to grain tithe, that he not separate from last year’s, born before Elul, for those born after Elul.
rashi:b16.3: And not for another matter: [such as] one type with its own type.
rashi:b17.1: One may not separate teruma: this speaks of the tithes of produce.
rashi:b17.2: Give the best of this and the best of that: that is, teruma and tithe, as it is written (Numbers 18:30): “when you set apart its best from it”; and the Merciful One says that he must give each one its own tithes separately.
tosafot:a1.1: Animal tithe etc.: everywhere it is usual to mention the firstborn, the tithe and the Paschal offering together, since their blood placements are alike. So the tithe is taught alongside the firstborn, and the Paschal offering, whose laws are many, is taught in Pesaḥim.
tosafot:a1.2: Is in effect in the Land and outside the Land: what we say at the beginning of Shiluaḥ HaKen (Ḥullin 138b), that wherever “in the Land and outside the Land” is taught it was unnecessary, except for the first of the shearing, refers to those taught in that tractate; but here it is necessary.
tosafot:a3.1: Rabbi Akiva says: Might a person bring up tithe, etc.: in Temura, at the end of Elu Kodashim (Temura 21b), Rabbi Akiva also says this, that a firstborn coming from outside the Land is not sacrificed. For there the Gemara establishes the mishna in tractate Ḥalla (4:11), that Ben Antigonus brought up firstborns from Babylonia and they did not accept them from him, as following Rabbi Akiva.
tosafot:a7.1: In accordance with Rav Huna, as Rav Huna said: a decree due to an orphan: Rav Huna’s statement is later in our chapter (Bekhorot 58b), at “How does one tithe them,” and there a decree due to diverse kinds, a tereifa or one born by caesarean section is not relevant. Here, though, a decree due to those would be as relevant as one due to an orphan; but since Rav Huna mentioned the orphan there, it is mentioned here. Yet it is puzzling that he does not say “a purchased animal and an orphan,” as he says there. So it seems to me that he mentions the orphan here specifically because people err about it more than about the others, since they are not expert in it, for an orphan too exists only where “this one departed to death and that one departed to life.”
tosafot:a9.1: Rather, due to a mishap: this implies that animal tithe is not in effect nowadays due to a mishap. Rabbeinu Tam asked from chapter Bameh Behema (Shabbat 54b): Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya used to tithe twelve thousand calves from his herds every year, and that was after the destruction. For Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who was Nasi, lived after the destruction, and after him Rabban Gamliel, and in Rabban Gamliel’s days they appointed Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya Nasi, as stated in chapter Tefillat HaShaḥar (Berakhot 27b), when he was eighteen years old. One cannot at all explain that it speaks of a tenth given to the king, like a tax [arnona]; and it is also strained to explain that he had a guardian who tithed for him when he was a minor. Perhaps they did not abolish animal tithe so soon after the destruction.
tosafot:a9.2: In brief: Tosafot explain that even according to the view that unspecified dedications go to the priests (Arakhin 29a), and even where one specified them for the priests, there is reason to decree due to a mishap, since as long as they are in the owner’s hands they are consecrated (above, Bekhorot 32a); in Avoda Zara (13a) Rashi explained that this baraita holds unspecified dedications go to Temple maintenance. As for Ulla in Arakhin (29a), “had I been there I would have given it all to the priest,” about the man who dedicated his property, one may say that case was land. Rabbeinu Tam asks how Rav Yehuda, who holds there that unspecified dedications go to Temple maintenance, permitted the property by redemption, “taking four zuz and throwing them into the river,” and answers that it was land, and forbidding land forever would lead all the more to a mishap. But that passage implies it was about movables, since it raises the teaching that a dedicated field applies only when the Jubilee applies, and answers “this is land, that is movables.” Tosafot answer that land outside the Land is called movables, as concluded there; and though the Pumbedita incident included land and movables, only the land was permitted, which fits the Talmud’s assumption that it included land, for had it been only movables he would not have permitted it. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a10.1: Money and metal vessels he should take to the Dead Sea: this implies specifically the Dead Sea, and other rivers do not suffice. So too it is implied in chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 28a) that in other rivers it needs grinding first, but into the Dead Sea one throws it as it is. And so elsewhere: one who set aside money for his naziriteship and died, we say he should take it to the Dead Sea. It is puzzling that in the incident in Arakhin (29a) it says he should take four zuz and throw them into the river, and likewise in Yoma, chapter Hotzi’u Lo (Yoma 55b), it says let us take four zuz and throw them into the river and let the rest be permitted. Perhaps there it speaks of grinding them. And now, when a person comes to redeem a fourth-year vineyard or fourth-year planting, he must grind the coins on which he redeems it and throw them into the river.
tosafot:a10.2: And what is uprooting? He locks the door, etc.: with a firstborn nowadays we would not permit doing this. Not only an Israelite, who must fulfill the mitzva of giving it and wait for a priest who wants to accept it, even more than thirty days for a small animal and fifty for a large one (for what we learned above, Bekhorot 26b, “how long is he obligated to tend to it,” applies even if a priest came to accept it within that time, as it teaches: if the priest said to him within that time, “Give it to me,” he should not give it). But even after a priest has accepted it, the priest is not permitted to shut it into a vault [to die], for nowhere is this ever taught regarding a firstborn. And above (Bekhorot 35a) we learned about a male sheep that is old with its wool hanging down, implying that they used to wait until it got a blemish. One may distinguish between a firstborn and one who consecrates nowadays: a firstborn becomes permitted once it gets a blemish, without redemption, so shutting it into a vault would be a loss to consecrated property; but what one consecrates is not permitted even after it gets a blemish without redemption, and if he redeems it he must throw the money away. Therefore when he shuts it into a vault nowadays, there is no loss to consecrated property.
tosafot:b1.1: It is possible, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: above in the first chapter (Bekhorot 3b) I explained that for us it is permitted to transfer ownership to a gentile, since we do not hold like Rabbi Yehuda [the print reads “Rav Yehuda”].
tosafot:b10.1: Consecration of value: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: the benefit he has from the altar’s sanctity he can give to Temple maintenance, and that benefit is that he could take a sela from another Israelite on condition that he give the animal to that man’s daughter’s son, a priest, to sacrifice it, as stated in chapter Ad Kamma (above, Bekhorot 27a). Thus far the Kuntres. But in tractate Arakhin (28a) it is explained differently, for we learned in HaMakdish Sadehu: a person may dedicate his consecrated items, whether offerings of the most sacred order or of lesser sanctity; if it was a vow, he gives their value, meaning their whole value, since he bears responsibility for them; and if it was a gift offering, he gives its benefit: [if he said] “this ox is a burnt offering,” they assess how much a person would pay for this ox in order to offer it as a burnt offering, which he is not obligated to do. And the benefit of chapter Ad Kamma applies only to something that is eaten, etc., for it is about such things that it is said there. Similarly it teaches in Arakhin (28b) about a firstborn: one may dedicate a firstborn, whether unblemished or blemished; and how does one redeem it? They assess how much a person would give for this firstborn to give it to his daughter’s son or his sister’s son. Alternatively: that kind of benefit applies to something that cannot be vowed or donated, but for something that can be vowed and donated the other kind of benefit applies.
tosafot:b14.1: The verse states: You shall tithe a tithe: here a juxtaposition comes and overrides the a fortiori inference, while above, in Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 33a), the a fortiori inference comes and overrides the juxtaposition, in the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, where Beit Hillel permit [the disqualified firstborn] even to non-priests; and there I explained it.
gershom:a1.1: Not in the presence of the Temple: after the destruction of the Temple.
gershom:a2.1: From a place where you do not bring up grain tithe: from outside the Land to the Land. Wherever tithe and teruma are written in the Torah, it means grain of the Land, since land or inheritance is mentioned beside it, for example: “For the tithe of the children of Israel which they set apart … I have given to the Levites; therefore I said to them, among the children of Israel they shall have no inheritance” (Numbers 18:24), and for example: “When you have finished tithing … look down …” (Deuteronomy 26:12–15). [So from there] you do not bring up animal tithe. And yet the mishna teaches that it is in effect in the Land and outside the Land.
gershom:a3.1: You may even say Rabbi Akiva: here, to be sacrificed; there, to be consecrated. When Rabbi Akiva says you do not bring it up from outside the Land, he means to be sacrificed; but it is consecrated even outside the Land.
gershom:a4.1: The language is also precise: that the verse speaks of sacrifice, since it is written “and you shall bring,” and it is from sacrifice that he excludes it, but not from sanctity.
gershom:a5.1: To be eaten with its blemish: and not when it is unblemished.
gershom:a6.1: If so, even nowadays: let it be in effect in our time.
gershom:a7.1: A decree due to an orphan: lest they bring it into the pen to be tithed, though it is not subject to tithing, as we learned in the mishna.
gershom:a8.1: Originally too: in the presence of the Temple too, [let there be no tithe] due to an orphan.
gershom:a9.1: It is possible by an announcement: that they announce that an orphan is not subject to tithing.
gershom:a10.1: Due to a mishap: lest he be unable to wait until it becomes blemished, and eat it unblemished. In the time of the Temple there is no concern about a mishap, since he can sacrifice it on high whenever he wishes, and he can eat it.
gershom:a11.1: One may not consecrate, nor dedicate, nor valuate nowadays: since all of these are for Temple maintenance, and it is impossible to store them away until the Temple is built, and one would come to a mishap with them. Therefore if he consecrated an animal, it should be uprooted, etc.
gershom:a12.1: If so: since tithe is not consecrated nowadays because we are concerned about a mishap, let us be concerned about a mishap with the firstborn too, and let it not be consecrated.
gershom:a13.1: This is what we are saying: let us transfer ownership of their ears to a gentile while they are in their mothers’ wombs, so that it becomes a partnership with a gentile and is not consecrated, so that one not come to a mishap.
gershom:b1.1: No: the firstborn is consecrated nowadays for this reason, that it is possible to act as Rabbi Yehuda says, inflicting a blemish on it before it emerges into the air of the world, so that it will not be eaten unblemished.
gershom:b2.1: There too, with tithe, it is possible to inflict a blemish on it from the outset, before the tenth comes out, so that it is blemished and there is no mishap with it; so let it be consecrated.
gershom:b3.1: Who knows which will come out, so that he could inflict a blemish on it from the outset? And if you say, etc.
gershom:b4.1: And they are common: blemishes are common among purchased animals, and unblemished ones fit for sacrifice are not common among purchased animals. Therefore it is prohibited to inflict blemishes on his herd, and for this reason tithe is not consecrated nowadays.
gershom:b5.1: One cannot change it from sanctity to sanctity: from a lesser sanctity to a stringent one, for example from a peace offering to a burnt offering.
gershom:b6.1: But one may consecrate them by consecration of value, and dedicate them. How? As we learned in Arakhin, chapter HaMakdish: a person may dedicate his consecrated items, whether offerings of the most sacred order or of lesser sanctity. If they are a vow, that is, he said [“it is upon me”], so that he bears responsibility for them, he gives their value to the priests, since he dedicated them. And if they are a gift offering, he gives its benefit to the priests. How? “This ox is a burnt offering” is a gift offering, since he did not say “upon me.” They assess how much a priest who is not of the serving watch would give the owner for this ox, for him to wait until the priest’s watch, so that he may offer it as a burnt offering and acquire its hide; and that benefit he gives to the priests when he dedicated them. Likewise one who consecrates his consecrated items by consecration of value, assessing them in money for Temple maintenance: if they are a vow, he gives their value; and if a gift offering, he gives its benefit to the treasurer.
gershom:b7.1: Lest you say there: that is why one cannot change it, since not every animal stands to be a burnt offering, as only a male is fit for a burnt offering; therefore it does not take effect on other offerings.
gershom:b8.1: But here: with tithe, every animal stands to be tithe, whether male or female.
gershom:b9.1: What difference does it make, if the sanctity of tithe takes effect on consecrated animals, on peace offerings? For what stringent sanctity is there in tithe that is not in offerings of lesser sanctity?
gershom:b10.1: To make it subject to “it shall not be redeemed” and “it shall not be sold”: offerings of lesser sanctity can be redeemed, and animal tithe cannot.
gershom:b11.1: [A printer’s note: the comments from “with new and old” up to “just as grain tithe” belong to the mishna.] With new and old, and they are not tithed from one for the other: those born before Elul and those born after Elul are not tithed from one for the other, the new for the old.
gershom:b12.1: For by right sheep and goats should not be tithed from one for the other: for if new for old, which are not diverse kinds with each other, and what is born of them is not diverse kinds, [may not be tithed from one for the other, then all the more so sheep and goats].
gershom:b13.1: The verse states “flock … all”: implying that all flock is one. That is, the “all” written in “all the tithe of the herd,” throw that “all” onto “flock,” so that it implies all flock is one; and sheep and goats are called flock, as it is written: “And if his offering is from the flock, from the sheep or from the goats” (Leviticus 1:10).
gershom:b14.1: Just as grain tithe is not taken from new for old: as we say in the Sifrei: “and you shall set apart from it”: from the best, and not from one type for another, and not from new for old. And teruma is juxtaposed to tithe, as it is written: “So you also shall set apart … from all your tithes” (Numbers 18:28).
gershom:b15.1: If so, new and old too: let them be included from “flock.”
gershom:b16.1: I juxtaposed it with regard to the year: animal tithe to grain tithe. Just as grain tithe is not tithed from one year for another, so too animal tithe.
gershom:b17.1: And not for another matter: that is, one may tithe from one type for another that is not its type.
